context.environment: Internet-facing web service (PayFlow HTTP API) - treat request bodies, query params, and headers as untrusted, even though this checkout currently only runs locally.
threat_model: Tenant-to-tenant data leakage (one user reading/modifying another user's records)

path_resolution: repo/file as-given (verified for sample of 6 including deepest and shallowest paths)

findings.title: Unvalidated q query param interpolated directly into raw SQL via $queryRawUnsafe
findings.description: searchTransactionsByDescription(userId, q) builds a raw SQL string by directly interpolating the caller-controlled q value into both a WHERE clause and an ILIKE pattern. The /search route has no validate() middleware, unlike the sibling / route. Query result columns are serialized straight into the JSON response, supporting direct UNION-based extraction of arbitrary data from other tables.
findings.exploit_scenario: GET /api/transactions/search?q=x') UNION SELECT id, email, password, 'x','x','x','x', "createdAt" FROM users -- exfiltrates other users' credentials/PII. q=' OR '1'='1 bypasses the wallet-ownership filter entirely.
findings.recommendation: Replace $queryRawUnsafe string interpolation with Prisma's parameterized $queryRaw tagged template. Add validate() with a max-length bound on q.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted, unstretched SHA-256 instead of a password-hashing KDF
findings.description: hashPassword computes sha256(plainPassword) with no salt and no work factor; verifyPassword recomputes the same digest for comparison. Every register()/changePassword() call persists this digest directly as passwordHash.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the user database is exfiltrated (via f001, a backup leak, or insider access), an attacker cracks passwords offline at billions of guesses/sec on commodity GPUs; no salt enables rainbow-table attacks across all users at once.
findings.recommendation: Replace with argon2id or bcrypt with a per-user random salt and tuned cost factor. Migrate existing hashes lazily on next successful login.

findings.title: deleteBeneficiary deletes any beneficiary by ID regardless of owner
findings.description: deleteBeneficiary(_callerUserId, id) takes the caller's user id as a parameter but never uses it. prisma.beneficiary.delete({ where: { id } }) has no ownerUserId filter. id comes straight from req.params.id with no ownership check.
findings.exploit_scenario: User A calls DELETE /api/beneficiaries/{id} with the UUID of a beneficiary entry belonging to User B. The record is deleted from B's account even though A never owned it.
findings.recommendation: Scope the delete to the owner: prisma.beneficiary.deleteMany({ where: { id, ownerUserId: callerUserId } }), check count === 0 to throw NotFoundError.

findings.title: Missing positive-amount validation on transfers allows negative-amount transfer to reverse money flow
findings.description: createTransferSchema.amount only enforces z.number().max(500000) - no .positive()/.min() bound. The insufficient-balance check balance.lessThan(input.amount) is trivially false for a negative amount, and Prisma's decrement/increment operators simply add/subtract the signed value, inverting both operations.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker with $0 balance calls POST /api/transfers with { identifier: victim@example.com, amount: -5000 }. The balance check passes trivially, the attacker's balance increases by 5000, and the victim's decreases by 5000.
findings.recommendation: Add .positive() and the same 2-decimal-place refine used in addMoneySchema. Add a defense-in-depth assertion inside createTransfer itself.

findings.title: getTransactionById fetches any transaction by ID with no ownership filter
findings.description: getTransactionById(userId, id) validates id is a UUID and fetches the caller's own wallet, but the Prisma query prisma.transaction.findUnique({ where: { id }, include: PARTY_INCLUDE }) is filtered only by the transaction's primary key, not by senderWalletId/receiverWalletId matching the caller's wallet.
findings.exploit_scenario: User A calls GET /api/transactions/{id} with a UUID belonging to a transaction between User B and User C (obtained via a shared receipt link, support ticket, or enumeration). The endpoint returns full transaction detail for B/C's transfer.
findings.recommendation: Add the ownership filter: where: { id, OR: [{ senderWalletId: wallet.id }, { receiverWalletId: wallet.id }] }, treating a no-match as 404.

findings.title: Unconditional leak of raw error message and stack trace to HTTP clients on any unhandled exception
findings.description: The fallback branch for any non-ApiError exception returns res.status(500).json({ error: { code: 'INTERNAL_ERROR', message: err.message, stack: err.stack } }) with no isProduction/NODE_ENV gate anywhere in the file. Every controller uses catch (err) { next(err); }, funneling all uncaught errors into this sink.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker triggers any exception not already converted to an ApiError (a malformed payload causing a Prisma type-coercion error, a transient DB blip, a programming bug). The 500 response includes the raw exception message and full stack trace.
findings.recommendation: Gate message/stack inclusion behind !isProduction; return a generic message in production.

findings.title: Dedicated auth rate limiter (authLimiter) is defined but never applied to any route
findings.description: authLimiter (limit 10 requests/15min) is exported but referenced nowhere outside its own definition. auth.routes.ts wires /register, /login, /refresh, /logout with only validate() middleware and no rate limiter. The only rate limiting these endpoints receive is the generic apiLimiter (300 requests/15min).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends up to 300 login attempts per 15-minute window against /api/auth/login with different password guesses, or credential-stuffs a large list of email/password pairs.
findings.recommendation: Apply authLimiter explicitly to the sensitive auth routes: authRouter.post('/login', authLimiter, validate(...), loginHandler) and similarly for /register and /refresh.

findings.title: Stored XSS via transaction note rendered with dangerouslySetInnerHTML
findings.description: The transfer note field is fully attacker-controlled by the sender (validated only as a length-capped string, no HTML/script stripping). It is stored verbatim as description on the transaction row, returned unmodified in the transaction-detail API response, and rendered via dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: transaction.description ?? '—' }} with no sanitization.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a transfer/top-up to a victim with note set to . When the victim opens the Transaction Detail page, the payload executes in their browser session.
findings.recommendation: Render the description as plain text instead of dangerouslySetInnerHTML. If rich formatting is required, sanitize with DOMPurify before rendering as HTML.

findings.title: Login endpoint distinguishes unknown email from wrong password via distinct error codes/messages
findings.description: login() returns UnauthorizedError('No account found with that email', 'ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND') for an unknown email, and UnauthorizedError('Incorrect password', 'INCORRECT_PASSWORD') for a known email with a wrong password. Both are reachable via unauthenticated POST /api/auth/login.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker scripts requests to /api/auth/login with candidate emails and a throwaway password, reading the code field to determine whether an email is registered.
findings.recommendation: Return an identical generic error for both cases and perform a dummy password-hash computation on the unknown-user path.

findings.title: verifyOrigin CSRF middleware is fully implemented but never registered
findings.description: verifyOrigin.ts implements an Origin-check CSRF defense, documented in its own comment as defense-in-depth CSRF mitigation. A repo-wide search shows it is never imported or app.use()'d anywhere in app.ts. The only actual CSRF protection live today is the cookie sameSite attribute.
findings.exploit_scenario: Combined with f018's permissive CORS, any host treated as same-site by the browser can have the Lax access-token cookie attached to a cross-origin request, with no Origin check in the pipeline to reject it.
findings.recommendation: Wire verifyOrigin into the middleware chain in app.ts before the routers; add a regression test.

findings.title: .passthrough() on updateProfileSchema lets attacker-controlled body overwrite passwordHash/email via profile update
findings.description: updateProfileSchema uses .passthrough(), allowing arbitrary extra fields through validation, which are then spread directly into prisma.user.update. Since User has real email/passwordHash columns, those field names survive and get written.
findings.exploit_scenario: PATCH /api/users/me { "passwordHash": "$2b$10$<attacker-hash>" } overwrites the victim's real password hash without their current password.
findings.recommendation: Remove .passthrough(); build the Prisma data object from an explicit allow-list of fields.

findings.title: changePassword never revokes existing refresh tokens/sessions
findings.description: changePassword() verifies the current password and updates passwordHash, but never calls revokeAllRefreshTokensForUser(userId), which exists in tokens.ts with a doc comment stating it's used on password change, but is only wired into the refresh-token reuse-detection path.
findings.exploit_scenario: A victim's stolen refresh-token cookie continues working after they change their password, up to the remaining refresh-token TTL (default 14 days).
findings.recommendation: Call revokeAllRefreshTokensForUser(userId) inside changePassword() after updating the hash.

findings.title: Access token duplicated into localStorage despite httpOnly-cookie design, undermining XSS mitigation
findings.description: Despite the app's stated 'no token touches JS' design, both register and login write res.data.accessToken into localStorage.setItem('payflow_access_token', ...). This token is never read back anywhere in the frontend but remains readable by any JS in the origin.
findings.exploit_scenario: Any XSS on the site (e.g. f008) can run localStorage.getItem('payflow_access_token') and exfiltrate it, defeating the httpOnly cookie design.
findings.recommendation: Remove both localStorage.setItem calls in authApi.ts; rely exclusively on the httpOnly cookie.

findings.title: lookupRecipient returns another user's email, phone, and live wallet balance from an identifier lookup
findings.description: lookupRecipient(callerUserId, rawIdentifier) resolves a recipient by email or phone and returns { name, identifier, email, phone, walletBalance } to the caller, with no relationship, consent, or beneficiary-list check required.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker calls the recipient-lookup endpoint with a list of candidate emails/phone numbers. For each valid PayFlow user, the response discloses their phone number, email, and live wallet balance.
findings.recommendation: Return only the minimum needed to confirm a transfer target; drop balance/phone/email from the lookup response.

findings.title: Access token returned in JSON response body in addition to httpOnly cookie
findings.description: registerHandler and loginHandler both call res.status(2xx).json({ user, accessToken }) after already setting the httpOnly cookie. This exposes the token to anything that can observe the response.
findings.exploit_scenario: A script running in the page context (via XSS such as f008, a malicious browser extension, or a compromised third-party dependency) intercepts the fetch/XHR response and reads accessToken directly from the JSON body.
findings.recommendation: Stop returning accessToken in the JSON body for the web login/register flow; return only { user }.

findings.title: TOCTOU race between balance check and debit allows concurrent transfers to overdraw a wallet
findings.description: Inside the prisma.$transaction callback, findUniqueOrThrow issues a plain SELECT with no row lock, the balance check runs against that snapshot, then an explicit 100ms sleep widens the window before the decrement UPDATE executes.
findings.exploit_scenario: A wallet with balance 1000 fires two concurrent POST /api/transfers requests, each transferring 1000 to different recipients. Both read balance=1000 within the window, both pass the check, both decrement - net effect: 2000 transferred out of a wallet that only held 1000.
findings.recommendation: Use a single conditional UPDATE (SET balance = balance - :amount WHERE balance >= :amount) or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / serializable isolation with retry.

findings.title: App runtime DB role granted CREATEDB, not just the migration/shadow-DB user
findings.description: setup-db.sh creates a single Postgres role payflow and grants it CREATEDB for Prisma's shadow-database workflow. This is the same role/credential the running application uses for all normal runtime queries.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the application's DB access is ever abused (e.g. via f001), the attacker inherits CREATEDB along with normal query rights, enabling disk-fill DoS or broadening foothold.
findings.recommendation: Use two roles: a migration-only role with CREATEDB and a separate unprivileged application role for the runtime DATABASE_URL.

findings.title: CORS reflects any Origin with credentials:true, unconditionally in production
findings.description: app.use(cors({ origin: true, credentials: true })) reflects whatever Origin header the caller sends and allows credentials, for every request, with no isProduction gate. env.CORS_ORIGIN is defined but never passed to cors().
findings.exploit_scenario: The access-token cookie is sameSite=lax with a configurable cookieDomain and no origin pinning at the CORS layer, so any host under the same registrable site is treated as same-site by the browser and can read the JSON response cross-origin.
findings.recommendation: Replace origin: true with an explicit allowlist built from env.CORS_ORIGIN, gated behind !isProduction.

findings.title: jsonwebtoken pinned to 8.5.1, the last version before several CVE fixes in 9.0.0
findings.description: jsonwebtoken <=8.5.1 carries CVE-2022-23540, CVE-2022-23539, and CVE-2022-23529. The app's actual usage signs/verifies with a single static string secret and no dynamic key-resolution callback, so the highest-severity vectors tied to dynamic key lookups have no direct trigger path today.
findings.exploit_scenario: Low direct exploitability today; the package is one dependency-graph change away from real exposure if a future code path resolves the verification key dynamically.
findings.recommendation: Restore jsonwebtoken to ^9.0.3; explicitly pass algorithms: ['HS256'] to jwt.verify().

findings.title: Registration endpoint reveals whether a specific email or phone is already registered
findings.description: register() distinguishes the conflict reason: existing.email === input.email ? 'Email is already registered' : 'Phone number is already registered', exposed via ConflictError code ALREADY_REGISTERED from the unauthenticated POST /api/auth/register endpoint.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker submits candidate emails to /api/auth/register and reads the response message to confirm whether that email already has a PayFlow account.
findings.recommendation: Return a generic conflict message that doesn't specify which field matched.

findings.title: trust proxy: 1 lets a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For spoof req.ip, potentially bypassing IP-keyed rate limiting
findings.description: app.set('trust proxy', 1) trusts exactly one hop of X-Forwarded-For. Both apiLimiter and the unused authLimiter key on req.ip by default. No Dockerfile/reverse-proxy config exists in this repo, so the actual deployment topology is unverified.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends repeated POST /api/auth/login requests, each with a different fabricated X-Forwarded-For header, bucketing each request under a distinct rate-limit key.
findings.recommendation: Verify the exact proxy chain in each deployment environment and set trust proxy to match precisely.

findings.title: No idempotency protection on transfer or top-up allows a client retry to duplicate a money movement
findings.description: Neither createTransfer nor addMoney accepts or checks any idempotency key. Each call unconditionally creates a new Transaction row and mutates the wallet balance.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user taps Send on a slow network; the request is accepted but the response is delayed/lost, so the client retries. Both requests independently execute a full debit/credit.
findings.recommendation: Accept a client-generated idempotency key on both endpoints, persist it within the same DB transaction as the balance mutation.

findings.title: Sender/receiver wallet ACTIVE status is checked before the transaction but not re-verified at the point of debit/credit
findings.description: The sender's and receiver's wallet status are each checked once before the DB transaction begins. Inside the actual prisma.$transaction block, the sender wallet is re-fetched but only its balance is checked - status is never re-verified.
findings.exploit_scenario: A fraud-review process suspends a wallet in the narrow window between the pre-transaction status check and the transaction's write. The transfer can still complete on a wallet that is supposed to be frozen.
findings.recommendation: Re-check status === 'ACTIVE' for both wallets using the freshly-read rows inside the transaction callback.

findings.title: verifyOrigin fails open when the Origin header is absent
findings.description: The check only rejects when an Origin header is present and mismatched; if no Origin header is sent at all, the request passes through unchecked. The middleware is currently unused anyway (f010).
findings.exploit_scenario: If f010 is fixed by wiring this middleware in as-is, any mutating request that reaches the server without an Origin header would skip the check entirely.
findings.recommendation: When wiring this middleware in, reject-by-default: require Origin (or fall back to Referer) to be present and match.

findings.title: Email fields have no max-length bound
findings.description: z.email() is used in registerSchema, loginSchema, and the shared identifierSchema without a .max(...) bound, unlike name and phone in the same schemas. The global express.json({ limit: '32kb' }) body cap prevents truly massive payloads.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers with an email value padded to thousands of characters before the @, potentially causing oversized index entries.
findings.recommendation: Add a .max(254) bound to email fields.

findings.title: Password hash comparison uses non-constant-time ===
findings.description: verifyPassword compares candidate === hash using native string equality, which short-circuits on the first differing character - a timing side channel layered on top of the already-weak SHA-256 scheme (f002).
findings.exploit_scenario: A remote attacker with very precise timing measurement could in theory attempt to recover hash bytes incrementally, though extremely hard to exploit over a real network.
findings.recommendation: Use crypto.timingSafeEqual on fixed-length buffers.

findings.title: Pino redaction list omits token/secret field names
findings.description: The redact.paths list covers password/currentPassword/newPassword/passwordHash and cookie/authorization headers, but not accessToken, refreshToken, token, rawToken, tokenHash, or secret. No current code path logs a full request body or token-bearing object.
findings.exploit_scenario: A future code change adds logger.debug({ body: req.body }) to a login/refresh handler for troubleshooting, and raw bearer/session tokens would be written to log files in plaintext.
findings.recommendation: Extend the redact paths to include *.accessToken, *.refreshToken, *.token, *.rawToken, *.tokenHash, *.secret.

findings.title: LOGIN_FAILURE audit entries store attacker-supplied email with no read/export endpoint
findings.description: On a failed login with a non-existent account, writeAuditLog stores the raw, unauthenticated, user-submitted email in AuditLog.metadata. No findMany/export route reads the AuditLog table anywhere in the codebase.
findings.exploit_scenario: No direct exploit today since there is no read/export endpoint. Risk would materialize only if an admin audit-log viewer is added later.
findings.recommendation: No immediate action required. If an audit-log read/export endpoint is ever added, ensure it's admin-only.
